The loss affects minimally disyllabic content words. [p. 3] ... For Kera’a, we can exclude the possibility of stress-based explanations. In [anonymised reference], we examine duration, intensity, spectral tilt, and measures of vowel reduction as possible cues of word stress in Kera’a. ... We do not examine pitch as a possible cue of word stress given that Kera’a is a tonal language. new_statements.rule_in_words: Kera'a (Idu Mishmi) is a tone language with five level tones of high functional load; acoustic measurement of duration, intensity, spectral tilt and vowel quality found no syllable consistently prominent, so the authors conclude there is no word stress. (Pitch was not tested as a stress cue because of the lexical tones.)
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed (no stress at all per source).
new_statements.exceptions: None. Second-hand note in Namkung 1996: 142 (from Sun et al. 1991, Chayu/Tibet variety) that the low-falling /31/ tone 'often becomes a weakened (unstressed) tone' in the first syllable of disyllables — a tonal-reduction remark, not a stress rule.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level; data from Midu (prestige) and Mithu dialects of the Dibang Valley, India; measurements on words, mostly minimally disyllabic content words; the detailed instrumental study is in an anonymised companion paper not yet published.
new_statements.identity_note: Kera'a = Idu Mishmi = idum1241 [clk]; the statement covers the Midu (prestige, Roing area) and Mithu dialects of the Dibang Valley, India. Chinese sources (Sun 1983, Jiang 2005, Liu et al. 2019) and the ZMYYC entry compiled in Namkung 1996 describe the Chayu (Zayü), Tibet variety, which they give four tones rather than five; no separate glottocode exists for it.
